“Assisted Living” Is a Label: How to Describe the Help Your Wife Needs Instead

A short guide to describing help in plain tasks, before anyone compares settings.

Download PDF

The social worker used three different names for places in one conversation. Each one sounded like an answer. None of them said who would help your wife on a Tuesday morning, or with what.

This guide explains why the name of a setting is a poor place to start, and what to describe instead: the help itself, in plain tasks. It explains. It doesn't say which name fits your wife. That belongs to the people who assess her.

A name tells you less than it sounds like

Assisted living, memory care and skilled nursing are names for kinds of places. What a place with one of those names provides is a separate matter. The National Institute on Aging says that some residential facilities offer only housing and housekeeping, while many also provide personal care, social and recreational activities, meals and medical services, and that in assisted living the exact arrangements vary by facility and by state.1

The Family Caregiver Alliance adds that these facilities may go by different names in your area, and that each state has different regulations for what an assisted living facility does and does not provide.2

So the first question isn't which name. It's what the next arrangement has to be able to do for your wife. That is a list you can begin, and her care team can confirm.

  • Start from what her care team has found during this stay and what you've seen at home. Keep the two apart on the page.
  • Where you aren't sure, write a question and ask for confirmation. Don't fill the space with a guess.

Describe the help in tasks

The Family Caregiver Alliance's discharge guide has a table headed “What kind of care is needed?” It runs through bathing, dressing, eating, personal hygiene, grooming, toileting, moving from bed to chair, walking, medications, managing symptoms, special equipment, coordinating medical care and visits, transportation and household chores, and asks beside each one who can help with it. That list is a fair outline of a day.3

For each task your wife gets help with, write what the help is: a hand on her, someone standing by, a reminder, or someone doing it for her. Then write when you've seen it needed. Include the early morning and the night; the same guide asks caregivers whether the person requires help at night.3

  • Write only the timing you've seen yourself or her care team has confirmed. Where you haven't seen it, write “not observed.”
  • A list of help is a description. It isn't a formal determination of anything, and nobody should read one into it.

Sort the essentials, and mark what's confirmed

Some of what a care arrangement provides is personal care: non-skilled help with bathing, dressing, eating, getting in and out of a bed or chair, moving around and using the bathroom. Some is skilled care: nursing care and therapies that usually require a licensed professional such as a nurse, doctor or therapist. That is how the federal Administration for Community Living's glossary divides it.4

Which of these your wife's next arrangement must provide is not something to work out at home. Write the supervision questions and the nursing or therapy questions as questions, and keep two columns: what her care team has confirmed, and what is still open.

Your own part belongs on the page too. The discharge guide says planners should discuss with you your willingness and ability to provide care, and that you should tell the discharge staff about any limits you have.3

  • Essentials are the help she can't manage without. Preferences are what would make life better. Keep them on separate lists, and keep her preferences in her own words.
  • What you can realistically keep doing is a fact for the page, the same as any other.

Carry the list into the comparison

When the time comes to look at places, each essential becomes a question. The National Institute on Aging tells families calling facilities to mention any special needs or preferences, and not to be afraid to ask questions.5

The Family Caregiver Alliance's advice is to look beyond the attractive appearance of the building and grounds and confirm that the care services you need are provided, and to be honest about her care needs and communicate them clearly to facility staff. A written list makes both easier.26

A Medicare guide for families says that before you make any decisions about long-term care, talk to someone you trust, like a family member, your health care provider or a social worker. The list is what you bring to that talk.7

What this means for your family

  • “Assisted living” becomes a list: which tasks, what kind of help, and when you've seen it needed.
  • Your part is to describe and to ask. Which kind of care or setting fits your wife isn't for you to settle alone, and it isn't for this guide.
  • Two places with the same name can provide different things (sources 1 and 2 below), so the same list goes to every place you ask.
  • The questions you can't answer by watching go to her doctor, her nurse, her therapist, the social worker or your care consultant.

What this guide doesn't do

It doesn't explain any medical condition, say which kind of care or setting fits your wife, or replace an assessment. What it says about settings and services comes from the sources below. The advice about what to write down is ours.

Ready for the next step?

You can now tell what a care setting is called apart from the help your wife needs from it. The care interview goes through every area of her daily life, including the parts that don't show up at home, and turns your answers into a Family Care Profile you can bring to any care conversation.
